passage:
My flatmate Kashish had two offers stuck to the fridge for a week: a steady analyst job in Gurugram and a two-year teaching fellowship at a hill school in Meghalaya. I watched her walk past them every morning with her tea.
On Saturday she sat at the table with a notebook and wrote at the top: "Kashish at 35: which one will she respect?" I pretended to read my phone.
She crossed things out and circled others. At one point she said, mostly to herself, "Either way I'll miss something. That's allowed."
By evening she had emailed the school a yes and the firm a polite no. Then she took both letters off the fridge and pinned only the fellowship one back up.
She's been gone four months now. Her messages are full of rain and children's drawings. Gurugram comes up only when she asks, "Ira, does the bakery downstairs still make those buns? Eat one for me."

qa.q: What were the two offers on the fridge?
qa.a: A steady analyst job in Gurugram and a two-year teaching fellowship at a hill school in Meghalaya.

qa.q: What might Kashish have been feeling when she said, "Either way I'll miss something. That's allowed"?
qa.a: She seems to have felt torn but accepting, letting some regret be normal instead of waiting for a choice with no loss.

qa.q: Which part of Kashish's way of deciding could someone else use?
qa.a: Asking which choice their older self will respect, then committing fully once it is made, as she did by pinning only the fellowship letter back up.

qa.q: How does Ira seem to see Kashish's choice four months on?
qa.a: Ira seems to admire it, reading messages full of rain and children's drawings and noticing that Gurugram comes up only as a joke about buns.

grounding: Shows a person asking which choice her older self will respect, accepting some regret as normal and committing fully once she chooses.

passage:
On the first snowy morning in Zaragoza, Mateo's class held a snowman contest in the playground. Hiroshi's snowman had pinecone eyes and a red scarf, the best one by far.
At break Mateo saw two older boys backing toward it, throwing snowballs and not looking. He could have shouted, "Watch out!" He opened his mouth, then closed it. They were big.
Crunch. The snowman's head rolled into the slush. Hiroshi stood very still, the scarf in his hand.
At home Mateo told his mum, "It's not my fault. I didn't touch it."
"And if you had bumped into it yourself?"
Mateo's face went hot. "That would be awful. I'd say sorry a hundred times." He looked at his boots. "But I didn't do anything."

qa.q: What did Hiroshi's snowman have?
qa.a: It had pinecone eyes and a red scarf.

qa.q: Why does Mateo feel it is not his fault?
qa.a: He didn't touch the snowman, so staying quiet feels innocent to him, though his hot face shows a flicker of guilt.

qa.q: What could Mateo do now to help?
qa.a: He could tell Hiroshi he is sorry he didn't shout a warning and offer to help rebuild the snowman, and next time call out even if the boys are big.

qa.q: What was it like for Hiroshi when the head rolled into the slush?
qa.a: Hiroshi stood very still with the scarf in his hand, probably shocked and sad that his best snowman was ruined while others watched.

grounding: Shows a child who feels less guilty for letting harm happen than he would for causing it himself.

passage:
Sports day practice ran late in the November chill, and the girls' hockey team waited on the pavilion steps for the school bus. Karan from 10B strolled past and picked up Jaya's taped-up shoe. "Did your grandmother play in these?" A few people laughed.
Deepika sat two steps above. She saw Jaya's ears turn red, saw her reach for the shoe and miss. Deepika's own throat felt tight. Say something, she thought. But Karan was loud, and it wasn't her he was teasing. She looked down at her phone.
"Ooh, tape, very fashion," Karan went on, dangling it higher.
The bus came. Jaya sat alone at the back, the shoe in her lap. Deepika took a seat near the front and told herself she hadn't said anything mean.

qa.q: What did Karan pick up?
qa.a: He picked up Jaya's taped-up shoe.

qa.q: Why does staying quiet feel acceptable to Deepika?
qa.a: Karan was the one teasing, so Deepika feels less responsible and safer looking at her phone, yet her tight throat shows she is uneasy.

qa.q: What could Deepika have done on the steps or on the bus?
qa.a: She could have said, "Give it back, Karan," sat next to Jaya on the bus, and told the coach or a teacher what happened that same day.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya when nobody speaks up?
qa.a: Jaya is left alone with the embarrassment and the shoe in her lap, and the silence may feel as if everyone agreed with Karan.

grounding: Shows a teenager who watches a teammate being teased and stays silent, feeling less responsible than the teaser while the harm still happens.

passage:
"Okay Sachin, you want the honest version? Fine. During Durga Puja the campus clinic put up that notice about the flu shot, remember? Free, five minutes, and the doctor said it was a good idea for hostel people. I walked past it every day for two weeks.
It's not that I'm against vaccines. I read about one person who had a rare reaction, and I kept thinking: if I take the shot and that happens, it's my fault. I did it. But if I get the flu, well, that's just the flu. It happens to everyone.
Then in November I got it. Nine days in bed, missed my practical exam, and Ma took leave to come and look after me. The whole time I felt oddly less guilty than if the shot had given me a sore arm. That's messed up, right? So Anirban here is booking a proper talk with the doctor this time."

qa.q: What did Anirban miss because of the flu?
qa.a: Anirban missed the practical exam.

qa.q: Why did skipping the flu shot feel safer to Anirban?
qa.a: A rare reaction from the shot would feel like Anirban's own fault, while the flu just happens, so doing nothing felt less frightening and less blameworthy.

qa.q: What would be a wise next step for Anirban?
qa.a: Anirban could have that proper talk with the doctor, bring up the worry about the rare reaction, and weigh it against what the flu actually cost.

qa.q: How was Ma affected by Anirban's choice?
qa.a: Ma had to take leave to come and look after Anirban, so the choice that felt like doing nothing still cost her worry and time.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding a recommended shot because harm from acting feels more blameworthy than a larger risk from not acting.

passage:
Last month, on the Hebbal site, I saw that one of the scaffold clamps on the third level was missing its bolt. Ujjwal, the foreman, waved it off. "It's been like that for days. Nothing happened."
I walked back towards the site office telling myself it wasn't my scaffold, and I hadn't loosened anything. Then a question stopped me at the door: if I had pulled that bolt out myself and someone fell, what would I call it? Not bad luck.
Walking away was also a choice. I just hadn't been counting it as one.
I rang the safety officer, Mrs Pinto, and she closed that section within the hour. Ujjwal didn't talk to me for two days. On the third he brought me tea and said the new clamp was his job now. I'm Binita, the junior engineer who slowed the work by an afternoon, and I'd do it again.

qa.q: What was missing from the scaffold clamp?
qa.a: The clamp was missing its bolt.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on the walk back to the site office, and what shifted?
qa.a: Binita felt uneasy but was calming that feeling with "it wasn't my scaffold", until picturing pulling the bolt out personally made walking away feel just as serious.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Ringing the safety officer worked, because the section was closed within the hour instead of waiting for someone to fall.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have seen Binita's call at first?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably felt annoyed or embarrassed, since the clamp had been like that for days, but by the third day he brought tea and took the new clamp on as his job.

grounding: Shows a young engineer who treats not acting as a choice, asks how causing the harm directly would look, and speaks up to the safety officer.

passage:
Saturday, Diwali holidays. Nikita, Deepak's cousin from Pune, scrolled through his phone and frowned. "This old quiz game had a data leak last year. And you use the same password for, what, twelve accounts?"
Monday. Deepak deleted the quiz game, cleared its data and even emailed the makers to close his account. "Done. Zero risk from that one," he announced, grinning. "The password thing is too much work. Twelve accounts, Nikita!"
"Changing just your email one would cut way more risk than deleting a game you never open."
"Yeah, but this one's finished. That feels good."
The next Sunday. A message popped up: someone had tried to sign in to his email from another city. Deepak's stomach dropped. The game was gone, but the door that mattered was still wide open. He called Nikita.

qa.q: How many accounts share Deepak's password?
qa.a: Twelve accounts.

qa.q: Why does deleting the quiz game feel so satisfying to Deepak?
qa.a: Getting one risk all the way to zero feels finished and comforting, so he feels pleased and safe even though the shared password is the bigger danger.

qa.q: What could Deepak do first once he calls Nikita?
qa.a: He could change the email password first, since that account can unlock others, and then work through the rest a few at a time with Nikita's help.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when Deepak says the password job is too much work?
qa.a: Nikita may feel frustrated, knowing that changing just the email password would cut far more risk than deleting a game he never opens.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing to remove a small risk completely instead of greatly cutting a larger one, because zero feels comforting.

passage:
The Dussehra fair had turned the village ground into a maze of lights, and Tejas, home from college, refused every stall. "Pani puri? No. That water could make me sick. I'm not eating anything here." He even rubbed sanitiser on his hands after touching the ride tickets.
At ten his friends waved him onto the back of a scooter already carrying two people. No helmets, and a dark road full of trucks back to the village.
Ritu, his cousin, caught his arm. "You won't eat one pani puri, but you'll ride triple on the highway?"
"That's different," Tejas snapped. "Everyone rides like that."
"Then everyone's wrong." She nodded at her brother's jeep. "Ride with us."
Tejas glared, cheeks hot, but climbed into the jeep and sat silently all the way home.

qa.q: Where did Ritu ask Tejas to ride?
qa.a: She asked him to ride with them in her brother's jeep.

qa.q: Why did Tejas snap at Ritu?
qa.a: He felt caught out and angry, because his careful food rule made him feel safe and he didn't want to admit the scooter ride was the bigger danger.

qa.q: What would you advise Tejas before the next fair?
qa.a: Compare the risks honestly: relax a little about the food, and never ride triple without a helmet on a dark road.

qa.q: How did Ritu see the scooter ride?
qa.a: Ritu saw it as far more dangerous than any stall food, and she cared enough to stop him and offer a safer way home.

grounding: Shows a student fixating on one small fear while ignoring a much bigger danger.

passage:
Two days before the Pune river run, Ankita's committee had money left for one last safety item, and the vendor needed an answer by six.
Deepika had a proposal ready. "We hire a second ambulance just for the bridge section. Then the bridge risk is zero. Nobody can ever blame us for the bridge."
Ankita pulled up last year's incident sheet. Two runners had stumbled on the bridge. Forty-one had needed help for heat and thirst, mostly between kilometres eight and fifteen, where the water tables were far apart.
"The bridge feels scarier," she said. "But three extra water stations and two first-aid volunteers along that stretch would cut far more of the total risk. The first ambulance already covers the bridge."
Deepika hesitated. "Zero sounded so good."
"It does," Ankita said, and signed the water order at five-forty.

qa.q: How many runners needed help for heat and thirst last year?
qa.a: Forty-one.

qa.q: What might Ankita be feeling as she compares the incident sheet with the proposal?
qa.a: She feels the pull of the bridge fear too, but she stays calm and focused on which option cuts the most risk overall, not which one feels perfectly safe.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Choosing the extra water stations and first-aid volunteers worked, because that stretch had far more incidents and the first ambulance already covered the bridge.

qa.q: Why might Deepika react differently to the choice?
qa.a: For Deepika, getting the bridge to zero sounded comforting and blame-proof, so letting it go may feel uneasy at first.

grounding: Shows a careful planner comparing how much total risk each option removes instead of chasing the comfort of a perfect zero.

passage:
Wanjiru had flown in from Nairobi to help with the baby, and within a day Ingrid noticed the pattern. Her mother-in-law kept the curtains closed and refused the park across the road. "I heard of a pram taken from outside a shop once. I won't risk it."
Yet that same afternoon Ingrid found a mug of hot tea on the low coffee table, inches from where little Amani was learning to pull up, and the blind cord dangling by the cot.
Ingrid felt a flash of irritation, then softened. Wanjiru's hands shook slightly whenever she spoke of the pram.
That evening they made tea together. "Your fear makes sense," Ingrid said. "Can we look at all the risks together?" They moved hot drinks to the counter and tied up the cord. The next morning they walked to the park side by side, Wanjiru gripping the pram handle.

qa.q: Where did Ingrid find the mug of hot tea?
qa.a: On the low coffee table, inches from where Amani was learning to pull up.

qa.q: What did Ingrid feel when she found the tea and the blind cord, and how did that change?
qa.a: She felt a flash of irritation, then softened when she noticed Wanjiru's hands shaking as she spoke of the pram, and chose kindness toward the fear.

qa.q: How did Ingrid help without dismissing Wanjiru's worry?
qa.a: She said the fear made sense, asked to look at all the risks together, and they fixed the common dangers before going to the park side by side.

qa.q: What is it like for Wanjiru to walk to the park the next morning?
qa.a: It is probably still frightening for her, gripping the pram handle, but she is doing it with Ingrid beside her after feeling her fear was respected.

grounding: Shows a young parent noticing a relative guard against a rare risk while missing common ones, and choosing safety steps together with kindness toward the fear.

passage:
"Saurabh, don't touch Dadaji's glasses," said Jagdish Dadaji, setting them on the stool.
Saurabh looked at the glasses, then toddled straight to the stool and grabbed them. "Mine!"
"No, no, beta, give!"
"No!" Saurabh hid them behind his back, grinning.
His big sister Chhavi giggled. "Dadaji, you said don't touch. Now he wants them more!"
Dadaji laughed and held out a wooden spoon. "Saurabh, swap?"
Saurabh looked at the spoon, dropped the glasses and banged the spoon.

qa.q: Where did Dadaji set the glasses?
qa.a: He set them on the stool.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh grab the glasses straight after being told not to?
qa.a: Being told no made the glasses more exciting, and he felt proud and pleased with himself, grinning as he hid them behind his back.

qa.q: What worked better than saying no?
qa.a: Offering a swap: the wooden spoon gave Saurabh his own choice, so he dropped the glasses by himself.

qa.q: How does Chhavi see what happened?
qa.a: Chhavi finds it funny and notices that saying "don't touch" made Saurabh want the glasses more.

grounding: Shows a toddler who reaches for something at once after being told not to touch it.
